findings.finding: The Scope section omits 'run scripts/gen_env_registry.py' as a required step, even though the plan explicitly acknowledges docs/env-vars.md is 'regenerated, never hand-edited'. The generator must be executed after the _permanent() entry is added to REGISTRY to make docs/env-vars.md reflect the REBAR_LLM_MODEL deprecation annotation; failing to run it will cause the CI drift gate (python scripts/gen_env_registry.py --check) to fail.
findings.location: Scope — docs/ bullet ('the generated docs/env-vars.md (regenerated, never hand-edited)')
scenarios: Implementer adds the _permanent() entry and commits without re-running the generator; CI drift gate fails on the stale docs/env-vars.md.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a Scope bullet: 'Run `python scripts/gen_env_registry.py` to regenerate `docs/env-vars.md` with the REBAR_LLM_MODEL deprecation annotation.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the preferred isolation mechanism explicitly in AC2 (recommend subprocess per the cited precedent at tests/unit/test_structured_run_seam.py:115, since the plan's own prose warns that reset-flag risks order-dependent blindness).
evidence: 'Use a subprocess (precedent: ...) or reset the once-flag explicitly in the fixture, and state which' — two mutually exclusive implementation paths, no default stated
The plan cites the subprocess precedent first and calls it out by file:line, which implicitly favours it, but does not make this the stated default
findings.finding: AC2 explicitly defers the isolation-mechanism choice to the executor ('Use a subprocess … or reset the once-flag explicitly in the fixture, and state which') without providing a default or tiebreaker. This is a real design decision — the two approaches have different trade-offs (subprocess adds overhead; reset-flag risks hiding real order-dependency bugs) — and leaving it to the executor means the plan is not fully executable without the executor making a significant design call.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria, AC2: 'Use a subprocess (precedent: tests/unit/test_structured_run_seam.py:115) or reset the once-flag explicitly in the fixture, and state which'
scenarios: Two independent executors pick different approaches, producing inconsistent test suites across related tickets.
An executor picks reset-flag and introduces an order-dependent blind spot the plan explicitly warned against — the warning is there but the plan still allows the inferior choice.
findings.suggested_fix: Change 'Use a subprocess … or reset the once-flag explicitly in the fixture, and state which' to 'Use a subprocess (precedent: tests/unit/test_structured_run_seam.py:115); do NOT use reset-flag, as the plan's own prose notes it risks the same order-dependent blindness the isolation is meant to prevent.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an explicit statement of REBAR_LLM_MODEL's CURRENT resolution scope (which class slots it currently affects) and, if the fan-out to all three is a net-new change, document an explicit rollback path (e.g., 'revert commit X' or 'set per-class env vars explicitly to override') so operators can recover without downtime.
evidence: 'Within the window REBAR_LLM_MODEL is still honoured, emits a deprecation warning ONCE per process, and maps to ALL THREE classes — the widest-compatibility reading, so an operator who set one model keeps getting exactly that model everywhere and nothing breaks mid-window.'
ABSENCE: the plan nowhere states what REBAR_LLM_MODEL currently resolves to (one class? a different mechanism entirely?), so the 'nothing breaks' claim cannot be verified from the plan text alone.
The fourth T4 checklist item requires an explicit rollback/back-out plan or expand-contract sequence, not just acknowledgement of compatibility.
findings.finding: The plan announces that `REBAR_LLM_MODEL` will 'map to ALL THREE classes' as the new behavior but never describes what `REBAR_LLM_MODEL` currently resolves to — which classes it currently influences and which it does not. If it currently affects only one class (or zero), the fan-out silently changes resolution for the other class slots from their built-in defaults to the operator-supplied value, which is a behavioral change. The plan asserts 'nothing breaks' and 'widest-compatibility reading' but provides no rollback path for the fan-out itself, and no explicit statement of current behavior to support the claim.
findings.location: Approach section — 'maps to ALL THREE classes'; Scope section — 'model_classes.py — the map-to-all-three fan-out'
scenarios: An operator currently has REBAR_LLM_MODEL set and relies on the OTHER two class slots using their per-class built-in defaults. After this change those slots silently adopt the REBAR_LLM_MODEL value, changing model selection without any config change on the operator's side.
A roll-forward-then-rollback scenario: if this commit is reverted after S8 has already shipped, operators using REBAR_LLM_MODEL lose the fan-out silently.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Approach or Scope section, add one sentence describing the current behavior, e.g. 'Today REBAR_LLM_MODEL is consumed in config.py as [single field / all three / etc.]; the fan-out is therefore [additive / a change from single to triple coverage].' Then add a one-line rollback note: 'If the fan-out must be reverted, operators can pin each class slot via REBAR_LLM_<CLASS>_MODEL explicitly; commit revert restores previous behavior.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify (in the ADR and in a dedicated test case) the per-slot precedence rule when REBAR_LLM_MODEL is set alongside a PARTIAL class-slot configuration — e.g., does the env var fill only the unset slots, or is it suppressed as soon as any class slot is present?
evidence: 'classes configured AND REBAR_LLM_MODEL set: classes win, warning still emitted' — treats all-or-nothing but leaves the partial case ambiguous
The AC test covers 'explicit class config' vs REBAR_LLM_MODEL but does not specify the per-slot granularity (e.g., COMPACT slot set explicitly, FULL and SHORT not set)
The ADR is required to record the class model and rejected alternatives — partial-slot precedence is a distinct decision that also belongs there
findings.finding: The business rule for PARTIAL class-slot configuration (some slots explicitly set, others not) is unspecified: the plan says 'classes configured AND REBAR_LLM_MODEL set: classes win' but does not clarify whether REBAR_LLM_MODEL fills the *unset* slots or is suppressed entirely once any class slot is present. This is an architectural decision that belongs in the ADR and needs a corresponding test case.
findings.location: Scope (model_classes.py fan-out paragraph) and Acceptance Criteria — 'classes configured AND REBAR_LLM_MODEL set: classes win'
scenarios: Operator sets REBAR_LLM_MODEL=anthropic:claude-3-opus and also sets REBAR_LLM_COMPACT_MODEL=bedrock:... but leaves FULL and SHORT unset — does REBAR_LLM_MODEL fill FULL and SHORT, or do all three inherit from the class-wins rule and revert to built-in defaults?
A misconfigured deployment silently uses built-in defaults for two of three slots when the operator expected the legacy var to cover them.
findings.suggested_fix: In the ADR, add a section 'Partial configuration precedence' that states the chosen rule (e.g., 'REBAR_LLM_MODEL fills any class slot that has no explicit value, regardless of whether other slots are set') and record the rejected alternative. Add a fourth unit test: one class slot explicitly configured, two not — assert the two unset slots resolve to REBAR_LLM_MODEL and the set slot keeps its explicit value.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify in the Approach section at which precedence layer `REBAR_LLM_MODEL` fans out within `_parse_slot` (e.g. 'replaces the built-in default only — CLI, per-class env vars, and config-table entries all win') and add an AC test for the partial-configuration case (some class slots set, others not).
evidence: Verified: `_parse_slot` applies per-field precedence: `_cli_override or _env_override or model` (line 156). `model` is initialized from `raw.get('model') or _DEFAULT_MODEL_BY_CLASS[name]` (line 148).

If `REBAR_LLM_MODEL` fans out as a replacement for the built-in default (`_DEFAULT_MODEL_BY_CLASS`), partial config works correctly. If it fans out at the env layer, it collides with `REBAR_LLM_<CLASS>_MODEL` for already-set slots.
The plan says 'becomes the default for all three slots at the point slots are built' — suggesting the built-in-default layer — but never makes this explicit for the partial case.
findings.finding: The plan's 'classes configured AND REBAR_LLM_MODEL set: classes win' AC does not define what 'configured' means per-slot, leaving the partial-configuration case ambiguous: if an operator sets `REBAR_LLM_FRONTIER_MODEL` but leaves standard and trivial unset, should `REBAR_LLM_MODEL` fill the two unset slots or should each unset slot use its built-in default? The fan-out layer within `_parse_slot`'s precedence chain (CLI > env > config table > built-in default) is implied but not stated.
findings.location: Approach section ('maps to ALL THREE classes'); AC line 3 ('classes configured AND REBAR_LLM_MODEL set: classes win')
scenarios: Operator sets `REBAR_LLM_FRONTIER_MODEL=anthropic:claude-opus-4-8` and `REBAR_LLM_MODEL=openai:gpt-4o`: should standard and trivial resolve to gpt-4o (REBAR_LLM_MODEL fills the gap) or to their built-in defaults? The plan's AC asserts 'classes win' but is silent on unset slots.
No test covers the partially-configured case — the three AC tests cover all-set, none-set, and all-or-nothing-classes-vs-scalar, not the mixed case.

findings.finding: The Approach section states 'migration window of one minor release,' but the Scope section states the deprecation is registered with `remove_in=_MAJOR` — a major-version boundary. These two formulations describe different removal timelines and would send an implementer in contradictory directions when setting the `_scheduled(...)` call.
findings.location: Approach paragraph 1 ('Deprecate with a migration window of one minor release') vs Scope/_deprecations.py bullet ('remove_in=_MAJOR')
findings.suggested_fix: Change Approach to read 'migration window of one major release' to match the `remove_in=_MAJOR` registry pattern already described in Scope.

findings.finding: The Approach section states the deprecation window is 'one minor release', but the Scope section cites `remove_in=_MAJOR` in `_deprecations._scheduled(...)`. These are contradictory: a minor-release window means removal at the next minor, while `_MAJOR` means removal at the next major. The ADR and operator expectations will be built on whichever wording is read, and the implementation will follow `_MAJOR` regardless — so the prose is misleading and the actual removal timeline is under-specified in the plan's own documentation criterion.
findings.location: Approach section ('migration window of one minor release') vs Scope section ('remove_in=_MAJOR, i.e. it WARNS and does not remove') and ADR AC
findings.suggested_fix: Change the Approach section to read 'migration window of one major release' to match `remove_in=_MAJOR`, and ensure the ADR uses the same wording.
